Transcribe every complete printed text line exactly, one array element per printed line, top to bottom. Preserve spelling, capitalisation, punctuation, printed abbreviations, section marks and end-of-line hyphenation. Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Syriac, Greek and Ethiopic must be Unicode text with every visible vowel point, dagesh, shin or sin dot, accent and diacritic, and with no point that is not printed; write them in logical order with no bidi control characters, keep the words of a right-to-left phrase in the order they are read, and keep the printed left-to-right order of separate items in a list. Transcribe the letters actually printed even when they are not the dictionary spelling: never insert or drop a vav or yod, and never replace a form with a more familiar one. Distinguish Arabic from Syriac by the letter shapes. If a line is only partially visible at the top or bottom edge, omit it entirely rather than guessing. Never add, reorder, translate, normalise or omit anything that is fully visible. If the crop contains no text, return an empty array.

lines.note: Final letter is ת (tav, with its distinct left foot), not ה; the mark under the kaf is a vertical two-dot shewa, not a single hiriq dot. Kaf carries dagesh lene, nun has qamets. Reading B matches; Reading A's כִּנָּה is wrong in final letter and first vowel.

lines.text: כַּנָּה f. (r. כָּנַן I) a plant, shoot, as be-
ing set, placed; comp. נָצַב, שָׁתַל. Ps.
lines.draft: ing set, placed; comp. נָצַב, שָׁתַל. Ps.
lines.reread: ing set, placed; comp. נְצָב, שְׁתִל. Ps.
lines.note: Both Hebrew words print qamets under the first letter (T-shaped mark under nun and under shin) and patach (flat stroke) under the second (tsade, tav) — נָצַב, שָׁתַל, matching Reading A; Reading B's sheva + qamets / sheva + hireq is not what is printed. Shin dot is at top right in both readings and in print.

lines.text: 80, 16 וְכַנָּה אֲשֶׁר נָטְעָה יְמִינֶךָ and (visit,
protect) the plant which thy right hand
hath planted. The ancient intpp. as-
sumed also the masc. כֵּן in the same
sense Dan. 11, 7; see in כֵּן II. 2.—Others
here make כַּנָּה imper. Kal with He pa-
ragog. from r. כָּנַן in a signif. to cover, to
protect; of which however there is no
other trace.
כַּנֵּה ἅπ. λεγόμ. Ez. 27, 23, Canneh, pr.
lines.draft: כַּנֶּה ἅπ. λεγόμ. Ez. 27, 23, Canneh, pr.
lines.reread: כַּנֵּה ἅπ. λεγόμ. Ez. 27, 23, Canneh, pr.
lines.note: Under the nun two dots are printed side by side (tsere), not a single segol cluster; the rest of the line is identical in both readings.

lines.text: n. of a city, prob. Ctesiphon, i. q. כַּלְנֵה
lines.draft: n. of a city, prob. Ctesiphon, i. q. כַּלְנֶה
lines.reread: n. of a city, prob. Ctesiphon, i. q. כַּלְנֵה
lines.note: Under the nun of the final Hebrew word two dots are printed side by side (tsere), not three (segol); the rest of the line is identical in both readings.

lines.text: which also is read in one of De Rossi's
Mss. Comp. יִקַּח for וְיִלְקַח; see more
lines.draft: Mss. Comp. יִקַּח for וְלֶקַח ; see more
lines.reread: Mss.  Comp. יִקַּח for יִלְקַח ; see more
lines.note: The second Hebrew word is printed with five letters: vav (sheva) + yod (hireq) + lamed (sheva) + qof (patah) + chet, i.e. וְיִלְקַח. Reading A drops the yod and mis-points (וְלֶקַח); Reading B drops the initial vav (יִלְקַח). The first word יִקַּח (with dagesh in qof) is correct in both.

12, c. suff. כִּנֹּרוֹתֵינוּ Ps. 137, 2, once

lines.note: The first syllable is printed defectively: the nun carries dagesh and a holem dot directly above it, followed immediately by resh — there is no vav between nun and resh (matching the defective plural כִּנֹּרוֹת in the line above). Only the second holem is written with vav (וֹ).

lines.text: כִּנּוֹרַיִךְ Ez. 26, 13; Gr. κινύρα, κιννύρα,
a species of harp or lyre, Lat. cithara,
[whence the modern word guitar,] a
stringed instrument of music, celebrated
for David's skill in playing upon it, and
employed both in sacred and profane
music, in rejoicing and in mourning,
Job 30, 31; usually as an accompaniment
22. al. Josephus relates, Ant. 7. 12. 3,
that the κινύρα had ten strings, and was
struck with a plectrum; but this is con-
trary to the words in 1 Sam. 16, 23. 18,
10. 19, 9, from which it appears that this
instrument was played with the fingers.
